name: Burkitts Reef ("Greg's Reef")
year: Construction Feb 1997 (2 days on-reef excavator work); first council application 1982 [R4][R8][R1][R6]
type: Existing natural basalt boulder headland reef, reshaped in place — boulders broken down/relocated with a rented excavator, not a new engineered structure [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
purpose: Surfing only — remove/relocate hazardous boulders and old rail-track debris that made the point break dangerous and largely unsurfable [R1][R3][R6]
size: ~300 m3 of rock moved; at least 12 large basalt boulders relocated/broken down; ~2.5 m local tide swing exploited to work at low tide [R4][R8] Shape model (07_scale/shapes/burkitts-reef-bargara/HANDOFF.md section 3; LOW confidence): the traced outline is the whole visible basalt rock platform on the Esri image of 2025-09-05 (registry img-08): area 31,485 m2, 321 m E-W x 377 m N-S (minimum values; the image frame cuts the polygon at the south). It is NOT the reshaped boulder zone, whose location is not defined in any source; the card's ~300 m3 and ~12 boulders are text values only and cannot be checked against the outline. Tide swing ~2.5 m [R4] has no datum.
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $6,500-7,500 (rough 1997 FX estimate, not sourced from an FX reference) ASSUMPTION A1: the 1997 AUD/USD rate (about 0.65-0.75) is the agent's recollection, no exchange-rate source consulted; effect about +-10 %. The AUD 10,000 itself is reported identically by R1, R4, R6, R8 but all trace back to Redgard's account (no invoice seen).
financed_by: Greg Redgard personally, who mortgaged his house; approvals only (no funding) from the Beach Protection Authority of Queensland and Burnett Shire Council [R1][R6]
motivation: One local surfer's grassroots push, not a council/tourism/erosion program: Greg Redgard, a Bargara Boardriders Association member, first applied in 1982 and spent over a decade lobbying before approval landed in 1997 [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
designer: Greg Redgard, a local sugarcane cutter with no engineering background or formal reef modelling/scale testing [R1][R4][R6]
contractor: None named as a firm — Redgard and his mates did the work themselves using a rented Kobelco hydraulic excavator [R1][R4][R6]
status_now: Still standing and still surfed as of the most recent (2024) coverage, known locally as "Greg's Reef"; no reported repair, damage, or removal in nearly three decades [R1][R5] Decision: verdict 'worked' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source, because every source found calls it a success; the evidence base is media and anecdotal (Redgard's own account, a researcher's before/after estimate relayed by R4, forum comments) with no monitoring data, so the verdict is of moderate reliability.
hover_text: A Bargara sugarcane cutter spent AUD $10,000 of his own money (mortgaging his house) to have an excavator reshape a natural basalt reef in 1997, after a 15-year fight for approval — surfable days rose from a handful a year to about 30, and the reef still works, unrepaired, almost three decades later [R1][R4][R6][R8].
design_as_planned: No formal engineering design, wave model, or scale test — Redgard designed and built it by instinct, telling ABC "Not rocket science, really, when you think about it" [R1]. The plan was simply to break down/relocate the boulders and discarded railway-track debris blocking the takeoff zone so a wave could "break over it," turning a hazard-strewn stretch into a rideable right-hand point break [R1][R6]. No modelled promises about wave height, beach width, or ecological effect were made [R1][R5][R6][R8].
as_built_vs_design: Because there was no formal design, sources report little planned-vs-built gap: construction (completed February 1997) matched Redgard's simple intent [R4] (February 1997 completion: R4; 'matched his intent' is the card author's reading of the absence of any reported gap). A Kobelco hydraulic excavator worked at low tide (using the ~2.5 m local tide range) to break down and reposition at least 12 large boulders, clearing a deep gutter that had split the wave into two disconnected sections, with gaps filled partly by hand — reportedly including carrying bricks out on a surfboard [R4][R6]. The Kobelco make and the 12 boulders are R4; the bricks on the surfboard are R6; the 'deep gutter that split the wave' detail is not isolated to one of R1/R4/R5/R6/R8 (paragraph-level attribution, the pages cannot be re-read here). Construction duration is reported two ways: [R4][R8] describe the on-reef excavator work as "two days (~8 hours)," while ABC News [R1] describes the whole job as completed "within weeks" of approval — a genuine, unresolved cross-source discrepancy the dossier flags rather than silently resolving. Some of the large rocks removed from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline rather than discarded, where locals still use them for fishing [R1][R4][R5][R6][R8].
outcome: Surfable days rose from "a handful" per year before the works to roughly 30 days a year afterward, with overhead (4+ ft) conditions on the order of 4 days a year, per researcher Andrew Pitt (SurfingRamps.com.au), cited independently via Raised Water Research and a Swellnet forum comment [R4][R8]. Wave face height is reported at 2-6 ft (0.5-2 m), period 7-10 seconds, described as a consistent peeling face that occasionally barrels [R4] (wave face and period; the 'consistent peeling' wording is paragraph-level, R3/R4/R8). Best swell window is November-April. The modification has held for nearly three decades with no reported maintenance, storm damage, or re-work [R1] (status as of January 2024; 'no reported' is a negative finding of this card). No coastal-protection outcome or ecological impact study was found (not a stated goal) [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8].
why_worked_or_failed: By the consensus of the sources listed in References (the card author's synthesis [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]; points (1)-(4) are inferences, not source statements), this is treated as a rare unambiguous success among artificial/enhanced surf reefs: (1) it reshaped an existing natural reef rather than importing new structure, unlike sandbag/geotextile reefs that must create a wholly new bathymetric feature; (2) it was a simple, low-risk intervention — removing hazards and gap-filling rather than engineering a specific wave shape, so there was little to go wrong structurally, unlike geotextile-bag reefs whose fabric tore, shifted, or sank; (3) a large natural tide range (~2.5 m) made the boulders workable at low tide with ordinary excavation equipment, without marine plant or diving contractors; (4) rock/boulder material is inherently more durable than sand-filled geotextile bags (general engineering judgement of the card author, unsourced here). No source reports a failure mode for this reef [R3][R4].
unexpected_results: Boulders cleared from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline, where locals now use them as a fishing spot [R5] — an unplanned secondary benefit. The project was picked up by TIME magazine (per ABC) as the "world's first surf enhancement project" [R1] and resurfaced in Australian national media in January 2024 as a good-news/DIY-hero story [R1][R7]. A marine-park dive site with the same name ("Burkitts Reef Dive Site", scuba/snorkel) is marketed separately [R10][R15]; it is NOT established that it is the same reef as the reshaped surf break: the image registry rejected the dive video as showing the natural marine-park reef, not the rock-reshaped surf break (03_images/reefs/burkitts-reef-bargara/images.json img-06, img-07; Lior 2026-09-25), so the 'two recreational audiences' reading and the dive site's ~9 m depth [R10] are not used for the surf reef. Redgard's daughter Tahlija, who grew up surfing the reef, became a professional surfer and credits it directly [R1]. No litigation, safety incident, localism/crowding conflict, or negative unexpected consequence was found in any source [R1][R5][R6][R10].
could_be_better: None of the sources reviewed (a negative finding of this card; including comparison pages that do critique other reefs' bag sizes, crest depths, and funding models) offer a specific critique of Burkitts Reef's execution — it is consistently used as the positive contrast case rather than a subject of critique. No critical surfer commentary was found. Sources suggest very little "could have been done better": if anything, some note it did not create "a world-class surf spot," only a modest, locally valued improvement — offered as a realistic-expectations lesson rather than a criticism [R3][R4][R8].
relevance_to_israel: Bargara's ~2.5 m tide swing [R4] is far larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast's tide range (well under 0.5 m, micro-tidal [R18], a web tide table) — Burkitts' construction method assumed tidal exposure that a Haifa-area site would not get, so similar reshaping there would likely need different plant (barge/crane, diver-assisted work) rather than simple low-tide excavator access (inference of the card author, unsourced). Bargara's 2-6 ft, 7-10 s point-break wave [R4] comes from a defined Coral Sea/Pacific swell season (Nov-Apr; the season is stated without a located source in this card, (unsourced)); Israeli Mediterranean wave climate is generally smaller and more wind-swell dominated with shorter period (general statement of the card author, (unsourced) here; Lior's Shikmona buoy readings are cited in the Albany card). The core transferable lesson is procedural/economic rather than technical: a modest, self-funded, reshape-what's-already-there approach (relocating existing boulders rather than importing new engineered material) achieved a multi-decade, apparently maintenance-free improvement for roughly AUD $10,000 [R1][R4][R6], in contrast to far more expensive professionally engineered geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere that have frequently failed or required costly renewal (comparison is the card author's, based on the other reef cards of this project). For any Haifa/Israel natural reef or rock outcrop with existing hazards, a similarly minimal clear/reshape approach is the direct analogy worth testing, if geology and permitting allow [R4][R1].

reviews.role: builder, Bargara Boardriders Association member, sugarcane cutter
reviews.quote_or_summary: You really couldn't surf it, because you'd take off, go for about 2 or 3 metres and you would just run into rocks.
The wave could break over it. Not rocket science, really, when you think about it.
He took Burkitts Reef, redefined what was possible and made what was once unrideable an absolute playground.

Assessed the reef's before/after performance: surfable days rose from "a handful... every year" to about 30/year, with the wave changing from a hazard-split break into a smooth peeling lip with some barrel action.
reviews.outlet: Raised Water Research spot page / Swellnet forum comment

reviews.quote_or_summary: Prior wave broke a few days/yr, now 30 days/yr plus overhead 4 days/yr — explicitly contrasted with failed professionally-designed reefs.

The surf break of Burkitts Reef at Bargara, in Queensland's Bundaberg region, was previously obstructed by large rocks. Then Greg Redgard and his mates turned the 'unrideable' beach into a surfers' playground.
